title: Introducing Biopharma Bench v0.2
summary: Raycaster introduces Biopharma Bench v0.2: new professional assignments, more realistic working environments, and further expert review of how we evaluate AI agents.
body_markdown:
Reading v0.1 runs, we saw agents treat the desk as a puzzle to solve rather than a job to do, and some of the cues were ours. In one clinical data reconciliation workbook, every row holding a discrepancy was marked “Ready for lock”. No clinical data manager flags individual discrepant rows that way; it pointed straight at the error. Now only the submission package as a whole is marked ready for database lock, as a real handoff would be. An informed-consent draft carried the parenthetical “(use the study contact block)” right beside the outdated investigator phone number we wanted the agent to catch. We removed the parenthetical so the discrepancy sits in the document without a signpost.


The prompts had the same problem. Early versions listed the failure modes the grader would check and dictated file paths like a test specification. Prompts now read like an actual handoff from a Regulatory Affairs, CMC, or Clinical Operations lead: drafting the response to a health authority’s Information Request, reconciling primary efficacy populations ahead of a BLA freeze, or setting the sponsor’s position across clinical trial sites before an FDA BIMO inspection. The agent works directly from the controlled folders, regulatory correspondence, and study records on the employee’s desk and records any assumptions in the deliverable.


The files gave the setup away too. Office documents still carried the stamps of the Python libraries that generated them, and file timestamps showed when we built the environment. We stripped the stamps and reset every timestamp to the environment’s date.


We also observed evaluation awareness: agents recognizing the evaluation setup and searching for grading instructions or previous transcripts. In one run, a verifier-related installation file prompted the agent to identify the setup as an evaluation and start hunting for grading material.


To keep the assessment focused on the work, we removed exposed construction clues and separated the agent’s workspace from the verifier. The agent produces its deliverable in one sandbox; grading happens in another, keeping grading instructions and reward outputs outside the working environment.


We also restricted external access so agents would work from the supplied records rather than search the web. Built-in web search and fetch tools were disabled, and outbound connections were limited to an allowlist of required services, such as model API endpoints. These restrictions constrain external access without making the environment fully offline.


We shared these observations publicly on X, tagging the Harbor team. Harbor subsequently published a[reward-hacking update](https://docs.harborframework.com/news/reward-hacking) describing further protections, including safer artifact transfers, removal of automatic verifier-log mounts, and neutral runtime names, alongside tools for checking tasks and reviewing completed runs.
